title: Rebuilding a monolith segment as an event-driven microservice
question: Tell me about a time you had to align conflicting stakeholders

situation: On the strength of my prior work, I was loaned for a year to a specialised cloud engineering team, tasked with moving a core segment of the on-premise C++ financial application into a cloud-native microservices architecture.
task: The goal was to port the application's logic into a new stack: Java, Kafka, JPA, Docker. But the on-premise application was tightly coupled, so we had to re-architect the service from scratch, from a blend of historical specifications and entirely new cloud requirements.
action: End-to-end implementation: I built the solution from the APIs, with proper error handling, through the domain logic to the database, using standard JPA data layers and event-driven communication with Apache Kafka. The domain itself centred on relationship management through InterAct messages, used for complex automated queries and structured XML messaging. I also introduced comprehensive automated unit and integration testing.

Pushback and alignment: some UX folks didn't fully grasp certain specific edge cases the feature needed to handle, so I had to push back on their specifications and help them align with the existing C++ implementation. I also helped the UI team work through integrating with the APIs.
result: Delivered the Java microservice on schedule.

challenge: Managing fragmented documentation and conflicting stakeholder requirements, particularly where the official requirements lacked the historical and technical context behind them.
hardestBug: An asynchronous data integrity issue during Kafka event replays. When certain business events were squashed by compaction during a replay, it triggered foreign key violations on linked entity deletions. I resolved it by refactoring the event-handling lifecycle and auditing data integrity at the application level during replays.
learned: Stakeholder management and conflict resolution, and how to communicate technical limitations to non-technical teams by aligning on shared project goals rather than on the constraint itself.
enjoyed: The move to modern practice: Docker, Kafka event streams, JPA, and the confidence that automated integration testing gives you.
